title: Blending Two IV Dextrose Solutions to a Target Concentration
context: A pharmacy technician needs to prepare 200 mL of a 9% dextrose IV solution by combining a 5% stock solution and a 15% stock solution. Two conservation rules -- total volume and total dextrose mass -- give a system of two linear equations in the two unknown volumes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Solve for x1 and x2 using the backslash operator, storing the result in vol (a 2x1 vector), and display it.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using fprintf, display the answer in the form "Use 120.0 mL of 5% solution and 80.0 mL of 15% solution."

% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc;

% a) Build A and b from the volume and mass-balance equations


% b) Solve for vol = [x1; x2] using backslash


% c) Display the result with fprintf
hints: "Total volume" gives one equation (x1+x2=200); "total dextrose mass" gives the other (0.05x1+0.15x2 = 0.09*200) -- write each equation's coefficients as one row of A, and each equation's right-hand side as one entry of b.
Once A and b are built correctly, MATLAB's backslash operator solves Ax=b in one step: vol = A\b, with no need to compute an inverse by hand.
The mass-balance equation's right-hand side is 0.09*200 = 18 grams of dextrose, not just 9 or 0.09 -- make sure you multiply the target percentage by the total volume before it goes into b.
solutionExplanation: Each physical constraint becomes one row of the system: the first row, [1 1], encodes "the two volumes must add up to 200 mL," and the second row, [0.05 0.15], encodes "the dextrose contributed by each solution (5% of x1 plus 15% of x2) must add up to the 18 g of dextrose that a 9%-of-200-mL target requires." Solving vol = A\b gives vol = [120; 80], meaning 120 mL of the 5% stock and 80 mL of the 15% stock -- a quick check confirms 120+80 = 200 mL total and 0.05(120)+0.15(80) = 6+12 = 18 g, exactly matching the target. The backslash operator handles this two-unknown, two-equation system directly, without the student ever needing to invert a matrix by hand.
concept: Formulating a mixing problem as a linear system Ax=b and solving it with backslash

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using polyval, predict the heart-rate change for a dose of 12 mg, storing the result in predictedChange, and display it rounded to 2 decimal places with fprintf.

hints: polyfit(x, y, n) fits an nth-degree polynomial to your data and returns its coefficients from highest power to lowest -- for n=1 that means [slope, intercept], in that order.

polyval(p, xNew) evaluates the fitted polynomial p at a new x-value, doing exactly what "plug xNew into slope*xNew + intercept" would do, but reading the coefficients directly out of p so you don't retype them.
p(1) is the slope and p(2) is the intercept -- keep that order in mind if you want to display them separately.
solutionExplanation: polyfit(dose_mg, hrChange, 1) finds the line hrChange ~ slope*dose_mg + intercept that minimizes the sum of squared errors between the line and the five data points, returning p ~ [0.39, 0.21] -- a slope of about 0.39 bpm of heart-rate change per mg of dose, and a small positive intercept near 0.21 bpm. polyval(p, 12) then evaluates that fitted line at a new dose of 12 mg by computing p(1)*12 + p(2), giving a predicted heart-rate change of about 4.89 bpm. hints: zeros(1, n) creates a 1-by-n row vector of zeros in one call -- that's your preallocated space, ready to be filled in the loop.
tic starts a stopwatch and toc stops it and returns the elapsed time; assign that returned value directly, e.g. elapsedTime = toc;, rather than calling toc twice.
Preallocating with zeros(1,n) before the loop means each x(i) = i^2 assignment just overwrites an existing slot in memory, instead of MATLAB having to resize the whole array on every iteration.

The first five elements of x confirm the loop worked correctly: [1 4 9 16 25], matching 1^2 through 5^2.

title: Detecting a Redundant Buffer-Dilution Recipe
context: A lab tech is given two buffer-dilution "recipes" that are supposed to independently pin down the concentrations of two stock components, but the two recipes turn out to carry duplicate information. You'll use the determinant to catch this before wasting time trying to solve the system.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The two recipes give the system: 3x + 6y = 30 and x + 2y = 10, where x and y are the two component concentrations. Build A and b.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Before attempting to solve, compute det(A) and store it in detA. Display it.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Attempt to solve for [x; y] using backslash anyway, storing the result in sol, and display it (MATLAB will issue a warning -- that's expected).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: As a comment, explain in 2-3 sentences what detA = 0 tells you about these two recipes, and why sol does not give a single trustworthy answer even though MATLAB returned some numeric values.

starterCode:
% Problem: Detecting a Redundant Buffer-Dilution Recipe
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc;

% a) Build A and b


% b) Check the determinant before solving -> detA


% c) Attempt to solve anyway -> sol


% d) Written explanation (comment)
hints: Notice that the second equation's coefficients are exactly 1/3 of the first equation's coefficients (3->1, 6->2, and 30->10 also follows that same 1/3 ratio) -- that's the algebraic sign of redundancy you're about to confirm with det().
det(A) = 0 is MATLAB's way of confirming a matrix is singular before you even try to solve anything -- checking this first can save you from misinterpreting a backslash warning as a "solution."

Because the second recipe is just the first one scaled down, there are really only 2 unknowns but 1 independent equation -- infinitely many (x,y) pairs satisfy both recipes at once, which is why backslash cannot return one single, reliable answer here.
solutionCode:
% a) Build the system
A = [3 6; 1 2];
b = [30; 10];

% b) Check the determinant before solving
detA = det(A);
disp(detA)

% c) Attempt to solve anyway
sol = A\b;  % MATLAB will warn: "Matrix is singular to working precision."
disp(sol)

% d) Written explanation:
% detA = 0 confirms A is singular -- the two recipes are not actually independent
% information, since recipe 2 is just recipe 1 scaled by 1/3. Because of that, there
% are infinitely many (x,y) pairs that satisfy both equations at once, so backslash
% cannot pin down one unique, trustworthy answer; the numeric output it returns here
% should not be read as "the" solution.
solutionExplanation: Checking det(A) = 3(2) - 6(1) = 0 before attempting to solve reveals a problem that a numeric answer might otherwise hide: this determinant is zero because the second recipe's row, [1 2], is exactly the first recipe's row, [3 6], scaled by 1/3, meaning the two equations carry duplicate rather than independent information. Since b follows that same scaling (10 is 30 scaled by 1/3), the system is consistent, but consistent-and-singular means infinitely many (x,y) pairs satisfy both recipes simultaneously, not zero and not exactly one. Backslash still returns some numeric vector along with a "Matrix is singular to working precision" warning, but that output is only one point on an entire line of equally valid solutions -- checking det(A) first is what tells you to distrust that single answer rather than accepting it at face value.
concept: Using the determinant to detect a singular (redundant) system before solving

title: Fitting and Interpreting a Grip-Strength Recovery Line

parts.label: d

% b) Solve the normal equation -> beta


% c) Fitted values, residuals, and R2


% d) Written interpretation (comment)
hints: weeks' (with an apostrophe) converts a row vector into a column vector; A_design then needs weeks and a column of ones side by side, both as columns, concatenated with a comma inside square brackets.
The normal equation beta = (A_design'*A_design) \ (A_design'*gripStrength) is the general recipe for a least-squares fit -- it works the same way regardless of how many columns A_design has.

R2 close to 1 means the line explains almost all the variation in gripStrength around its mean; you don't need to compare it to any other model here to interpret it -- just look at how close it is to 1.

Computing R2 = 1 - SSres/SStot compares how much of the total spread in gripStrength around its mean is left unexplained by the fitted line (SSres) versus the total spread itself (SStot); here R2 ~ 0.997, meaning the line accounts for about 99.7% of the variation in the data, which is about as strong a linear trend as you could hope to see in real recovery data. A value this close to 1 suggests a straight line is a very reasonable model for this patient's short-term recovery, without needing to try a more complex model.

parts.label: d

% b) Loop-based deviation -> devLoop


% c) Vectorized deviation -> devVec, confirm match


% d) Logical indexing -> artifacts
hints: hr - avgHR works directly on the whole vector at once, subtracting avgHR from every element in a single expression -- no loop needed for that version.
isequal(devLoop, devVec) returns true only if every corresponding element matches exactly; since both methods do the exact same arithmetic, they should agree exactly here.

abs(devVec) > stdHR produces a logical vector the same size as hr, and using that logical vector directly inside hr(...) returns only the actual hr values at the flagged positions -- this is logical indexing, not a search function like find().
solutionExplanation: devLoop and devVec compute the exact same quantity -- each reading's distance from avgHR -- but devVec does it in one vectorized expression, hr - avgHR, which subtracts the scalar avgHR from every element of hr simultaneously rather than one element at a time in a loop; isequal confirms they produce identical results, since both are doing the same underlying arithmetic. abs(devVec) > stdHR then builds a logical vector flagging any reading whose deviation from the mean exceeds one standard deviation, and using that logical vector directly as an index into hr -- hr(abs(devVec) > stdHR) -- returns only the flagged readings themselves, [130 129], in one step without a loop or a separate find() call. Both of the obviously implausible readings (130 and 129 bpm, likely motion artifacts) get caught by this single vectorized filter.
concept: Vectorized arithmetic versus an equivalent loop, combined with logical indexing to filter data

% Name:

% a) Build the system, check rank and determinant


% b) Solve for x


% c) Condition number

hints: rank(A) only tells you whether A is technically invertible (full rank) or not -- it does not distinguish between a matrix that's comfortably invertible and one that's invertible "by a hair," which is exactly the distinction cond(A) is built to capture.

Look closely at A's first two rows: [1 2 1] and [2 4.001 2] -- the second is almost exactly double the first, differing only in the middle entry by 0.001. That near-duplication is what makes this matrix nearly singular despite technically having full rank.

Perturbing only the second entry of b (the measurement tied to that almost-duplicate row) and comparing norm(x_pert - x) to the unperturbed solution's own scale will show just how disproportionate the resulting change is.
solutionExplanation: rank(A) returns 3, confirming A is technically invertible and satisfying the textbook requirement for Ax=b to have a unique solution, and det(A) is a small but nonzero 0.002 -- also technically consistent with invertibility. Yet cond(A) comes out to roughly 37,000, revealing that A sits extremely close to the boundary of being singular, because its first two rows, [1 2 1] and [2 4.001 2], are nearly exact multiples of one another (row 2 is almost precisely 2x row 1, differing only by 0.001 in the middle entry) -- two of the three "independent" experiments are nearly measuring the same thing. The core lesson is that rank is a yes/no test for invertibility, while cond is a continuous measure of how close to "no" a technically-"yes" answer actually is; a full-rank matrix can still be numerically untrustworthy, so any real identification problem needs both checks, not rank alone.

context: A lab is setting up three different diagnostic-panel systems, each meant to solve for two unknown reagent concentrations from two measurements. starterCode:
% Problem: Classifying Existence and Uniqueness Across Three Diagnostic Panels
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc;

% a) Panel 1: expect a unique solution


% b) Panel 2: expect no solution

hints: Compute all three determinants before trying to interpret any of the backslash results -- det(A1) not equal to 0 signals Panel 1 is the well-behaved case, while det(A2) = det(A3) = 0 signals both remaining panels are singular in the same way.

For the two singular panels, look at whether b is a scaled multiple of the same ratio that makes A's rows proportional: A2 and A3 share the exact same rows, [2 3] and [4 6] (row 2 is exactly 2x row 1), so the deciding factor is whether each b vector also follows that same 2x ratio between its two entries.

In Panel 2, b2 = [5; 9] does NOT follow the 2x ratio (9 is not 2x5), meaning the two equations contradict each other -- no point can satisfy both. In Panel 3, b3 = [5; 10] DOES follow it (10 is exactly 2x5), meaning the second equation adds no new information at all -- every point satisfying the first equation automatically satisfies the second too.
solutionCode:
% a) Panel 1: expect a unique solution
A1 = [3 2; 1 4];
b1 = [16; 18];
det1 = det(A1);
disp(det1)
x1 = A1\b1;
disp(x1)

% b) Panel 2: expect no solution
A2 = [2 3; 4 6];
b2 = [5; 9];
det2 = det(A2);
disp(det2)
x2 = A2\b2;   % MATLAB warns: matrix is singular
disp(x2)

% c) Panel 3: expect infinitely many solutions
A3 = [2 3; 4 6];
b3 = [5; 10];
det3 = det(A3);
disp(det3)
x3 = A3\b3;   % MATLAB warns: matrix is singular
disp(x3)

% d) Written explanation (Panels 2 vs 3):
% A2 and A3 are the identical matrix, with row 2 exactly 2x row 1 in both cases, so both
% determinants are 0 and neither panel has a unique solution. The difference is entirely
% in b: b2 = [5;9] does NOT scale by that same factor of 2 (9 is not 2*5), so the two
% equations describe parallel, non-intersecting lines -- no (x,y) pair can satisfy both,
% hence no solution. b3 = [5;10] DOES scale by exactly 2 (10 = 2*5), so the second equation
% is a redundant restatement of the first -- every point on that one line satisfies both
% equations, hence infinitely many solutions.

% e) Written connection to imaging:
% In CT reconstruction, each X-ray measurement is one equation constraining the unknown
% tissue-density values, and the image is only fully determined if there are at least as
% many independent measurements as unknowns. If a patient can only tolerate a limited
% number of X-ray angles (for radiation-dose or time reasons), the resulting system is
% genuinely underdetermined -- not because of a math error, but because of a real physical
% limitation -- so infinitely many different tissue-density images could all satisfy the
% measurements equally well. Picking any one of them without additional assumptions
% (regularization) risks reconstructing a plausible-looking image that isn't actually the
% patient's real anatomy, which is a patient-safety concern, not just a curiosity.
solutionExplanation: Panel 1 has det(A1) = 10, nonzero, so backslash returns a single well-defined solution, x1 = [2.8; 3.8]. Panels 2 and 3 share the exact same coefficient matrix, [2 3; 4 6], whose rows are proportional (row 2 is exactly 2x row 1), giving det = 0 for both -- but their outcomes diverge based on b: b2 = [5; 9] breaks that same 2x proportionality (9 is not 2x5), making the two equations contradictory (parallel, non-intersecting lines), so Panel 2 has no solution, which is why MATLAB's backslash returns an Inf/-Inf-flavored output along with a singularity warning. b3 = [5; 10], on the other hand, does follow the 2x proportionality (10 = 2x5), so Panel 3's second equation is just a restatement of the first -- the two lines are identical, and infinitely many (x,y) pairs satisfy both at once, which is why backslash returns a warning plus a not-fully-meaningful numeric answer rather than the one true infinite solution set. The imaging connection matters because CT reconstruction turns exactly this same math into a patient-safety issue: too few independent X-ray measurements relative to unknown tissue densities produces a genuinely underdetermined system, and picking just one of the infinitely many mathematically-valid reconstructions without additional constraints (regularization) risks displaying an image that looks plausible but doesn't reflect the patient's actual anatomy.
concept: Classifying existence/uniqueness of linear-system solutions via determinant and consistency, applied to medical imaging

Look at the actual signs of r_lin in order, not just their magnitudes -- a run of same-signed residuals followed by a run of the opposite sign (rather than the signs flipping back and forth unpredictably) is the tell-tale mark of a systematic pattern, not random noise.

For the extrapolation, evaluate your quadratic model at dose=30 using the same three-term formula (beta_quad(1)*30^2 + beta_quad(2)*30 + beta_quad(3)) that you used to build the design matrix -- percent viability can never be negative in reality, so pay close attention to the sign of the result.
solutionExplanation: The linear fit's residuals, r_lin, run negative for the first two doses, positive through the middle five, and negative again for the last two -- a clear hump-shaped pattern rather than random up-and-down noise, which is the classic sign that a straight line is missing real curvature in the underlying relationship (here, R2_lin is still a respectable 0.9493, showing that a decent-looking R2 alone can mask a systematic misfit that the residual pattern reveals immediately). Adding a dose-squared term lets the quadratic model capture that curvature, raising R2_quad to about 0.9996 and leaving residuals with no discernible pattern in sign. However, evaluating that same quadratic model at dose = 30 Gy -- nearly double the highest observed dose of 16 Gy -- gives extrapolated of about -53.5%, a physically impossible negative viability percentage, because the fitted quadratic curve was only ever constrained to match data between 0 and 16 Gy and continues curving downward without limit past that range. This is the core danger of extrapolation: R2 measures how well a model describes the data it was trained on, not whether the model's mathematical form remains meaningful outside that range, so a high-R2 polynomial fit should never be trusted to predict conditions well beyond the doses actually tested.
concept: Reading residual patterns to detect model misspecification, and recognizing the danger of extrapolating a polynomial fit beyond its data range
